blocks.x: This is Bill Russover interviewing Charles Hamilton over at 732 St. Peter Street. And the date is March the 21st, 1965. Can you give your full name if you have a middle name?
Yeah, my full name is Charles Joseph Hamilton.

Texas, that was our territory. We done good. Well, I had a chance to meet a lot of guys and get a lot of experience in music, along in that line. And a lot of the musicians I met and sang, a lot of boys from Alexander, John Duncan, Zeb, and Tav Krohn, a lot of the fellas around there. And there was a bunch of fellas there now from Elorade around there, Leonard Parker, and there was a fine little excellent banjo player around there, and we called him Baby Buster. And he was a guy, he picked a lot of solos, and he was fast. And there was some boys who used to come there in winter after the show, the Rabbit Foot Show and the Silas Green Show. The musicians, most of them, would winter in Monroe, and I had a chance to meet all those guys, and I learned a lot of things from those guys they showed me. So I left after the band, Harry Walker took the band over, and I went on to Hot Springs. I went over there and played over there at a nightclub over there with another bunch of fellas around there, at Wilson's Place down on Melvin Avenue. And I stayed over there about four months in Hot Springs. We played, they were rocking. Well, his nightclub was in, it was a seasonable place, and certain seasons when the tourists would be there, you'd have a nightclub down there. So I played down there about three months, and well after the season closed I went back to Monroe.
Who were the best banjo players here in New Orleans when you were young, when you were a kid, even before you took it up? Can you, anybody that you watched or liked?
Well it was a fella, there were two fellas that I know, one of them was one of those Marrero, but it wasn't Lawrence.
John.

It wasn't John Marrero. I used to call him Ruth Gordon, and yeah, him. And there was another fella, oh he was fast, and he was a younger boy, he was wild. I mean, I think he was a sincere, Poise Sevier. Poise Sevier, yeah, I've heard George Williams about him. Poise Sevier, yeah, oh he was just fast, he was fast as lightning. But he had a different style in those fellas, and I had met him in Natchez later, years after I left here. But those were about the two, well I never did pay much attention to banjo players much during in them days. Did you ever play guitar, by the way?
Did you ever take up the guitar? No, I never take up the guitar.

Because when, after I left that part of the country up there, and I came down there, it was around, getting around in the Depression time, and the people were putting the banjoes down for the ghettos. And I wasn't able to buy a ghetto, so I went back on the piano. And while I was before, while I was up around Monroe, there was some fine banjo players up there I met. And so after these, these majestic ramblers broke up, so Ben Boyden, saxophone player, said, let's you and I organize a band. I said, man, I want you on piano, because you've been around Hot Spring and you done caught on a lot of styles and playing different. I said, you just kind of playing the kind of style of piano I want. I said, well I'll tell you how I learned. I said, I had been listening around there, listening to Earl Hines play a lot, and I said, I got a lot of his record, and I like his style. I said, I stand up there and watched him poison him. I said, and he's so far ahead of his time. I said, I'd like to pick up a style like that. He said, well we go ahead and organize a band and we're going to build it around you. And you just play out and we just play harmony and we build a band around you. So we done that. And I stayed around about four years, just playing the piano with the band, you know. And I was the feature man in the band. So, well, around about 32, 33, 34, things began to get tough out there. The Depression was hitting around that part of the country. It hadn't been there before. And I said, well, I got me a few dollars. I said, I had got married about two years before that. I said, I think I'm going to go back to New Orleans. I said, because, I said, since I'm married, I said, I have a wife. I got something to look out to. And I said, my mother and them, they got a big home now and then. And if I could happen to fall through, I say, I got to take care of this good. So, we left, packed up, left in 1934. And I came back to New Orleans. And I stayed around here a pretty long while. I didn't have nothing to do. And then the WPA opened up. I couldn't get on or nothing. So finally in 19, around about, oh I used to play a little job. I played with George Lewis. I played with different guys. They'd hire me for what I did. I played with Andy, Kid Howard, around in the 30s. When they get a job, they play the banjo and the avatar. When they have the piano, I play the piano. I played at the voice camp back there. There was the players back there, Willie Unfrey was band leader back there. There was the cabaret back there on Basin Street back up there.
In the district there? Yeah.
I played there a couple of nights. And the entertainers, that was the name of the place, the entertainers.
I had a picture there.

Yeah, I played in there, with Willie and them. Well, I got right smart away, but still it wasn't enough to do any good. And it was a good while before guys knew that you were back in town. So I went on and I played around with Howard. Then I started going, making trips with Isaiah Morgan, with Sam Morgan's brother, the Buggaloos. Sam and other people. Sam and different places. And with George William. And finally I got on the WPA, not in the band, but I got on the WPA project down there, on the music project. Well they had a great big band.
A lot of the musicians were in there. Were you in that too?

Oh, they were in the big band. No, I wasn't in the band. I never did get on, because it was late 40s and they was about to break the band. But I was the porter at the music studio down on Almonaster and Royal. They had a big building there. The teachers used to come there and teach the pupils. And Said, brother and I, were the porter there. They had a brother named Ellick. Said, Said.
He has a piano, a brother plays piano too. I haven't seen him through a while. Well Ellick used to play piano too. You see an older brother?

Ellick had lost one of his eyes. I never knew him. Yeah, no he died right after we were working on it. And he used to tell me we had already had around about 20 pianos in that building. And we used to go out and pick out the one that had the best tone and we played on there. And we used to play the music ourselves, we were getting paid. Well after WPA went out into existence I got a job down at the podium vacation. Well that kind of made a difference in my music career.
You didn't play as much. Couldn't play as much.

I was working on a job where I had more security, and because the music, one time you would make it, and one time we didn't. And a lot of times the jobs were going all the town, and I couldn't go all the town. And up until then I went and worked with Cottrell, Oscar Ruzon, a fellow named Joe Phillip, he organized a band after Sidney Desvign. Oh we had a very refined band. And I worked with Hill Hoever Lyric, and I started playing piano again with those guys. And I stayed in the band until Joe Phillips got rid of the band and turned it over to a fellow named Houston. Well Houston was the piano player himself, William Houston, professor and school teacher. His one has the music still. Yeah, quite naturally he couldn't use me. He played himself. So I went out and played with Raymond and different fellows around here. And I started playing around in Dixieland again. I met, I started working a couple of nights at the pad office. And I was playing with rock and roll groups. And I said, well, I worked down at the port about 23 years. I said, well, I can't, can't never get off to go. I think in certain couple of times I made a couple of trips through up there in New England states with George Lewis. I get off like a week or so or two weeks. And I had, but I didn't have a chance to get out in the line like to meet the other musicians and get around too much on the counter of my wife. So last June, things were, I get on there and I went on pension down there. And I said, well, I have a chance right now to get out of there. But that had been why I had been so further back and, you know, kind of unknown to a lot of fellas because a lot of them wouldn't venture to call me because they knew I couldn't get off from my job to play regular and going and I couldn't take no regular job. So then after that, I started, Kimmel came up there and asked me about playing with him. Well, the two jobs that I was playing with, with the big band, the 12 piece band, and they were, the jobs were conflicting because it was in the carnival season and they had a lot of balls. And Kimmel's job was on Friday and Saturday and their job was on Friday and Saturday. So I said, well, in the big band, I had to go to rehearsal probably every week, sometimes twice a week and play two nights or three nights. And then there was so much rehearsal and it kept me so busy. I said, I'm just going to join the Dixieland group. So I went on and I was playing with Kimmel and I was playing at the paddock.
Do you like piano better than band?

Yeah, since I, since, yeah, late, I would rather play the piano than banjo because I had been off it so long and after you get a certain age and you don't stay on those instruments, I mean, you get dramatism in your hands and fingers and things. And I wouldn't, I could play and make the chords but I wouldn't be able to play the style and things like I played years back.
Yeah, I never knew you played banjo.
And I have made some recordings for, on a banjo and some recordings on, with the piano and with, what do you call it, with Kent? The brother used to, with Mills.
With Mills. Yeah, yeah. That's the first time I heard you play banjo. I believe that you did.

Well the first time I went up there, up there in New Hampshire, I stayed at some musician's house up there and they say, well you a piano player, said we have some records here, with a Charlie Hamilton playing banjo. I said, well that's me, I'll play it on there. I said, but I never had one at the record. Yeah. And he was Mills, because he was supposed to send us some, but we never did hear from him after he went to California.
Yeah, I haven't seen him before.

And these fellas up there had the records. And they wanted to give it to me, and he said, well this all I have. I said, well no I don't want to take it. He said, well we are proud of this record. It was a one track on an album, a long album in here.
Yeah, I remember when you, I was there when you made that one time.
Yeah, and that was nice.
Uh huh. Oh, one more question about the piano. Did you ever have any real lessons, aside from your mother helping you some?

Yeah, I had lessons up around there, but I'll tell you one thing, after you have studied a whole lot, and get a lot down in your head, without lessening and things, and you can learn and get a lot of the lessons in your head and everything. But, and learn how to read the music on there, and how to divide the division and everything. But, one thing, you can go a certain distance in that, and as far as you can go. Because, I mean, first thing, your fingering and everything, you got that already, and it's artificial, and it's already contrary to the music part of it. Yeah. So it's nice to learn how to read the music. I mean, just play it, and pick out the melody, and you go ahead and play it the way you want. Yeah, where you like to hear it. You just have your chords, and your keys, and the vision in it, and then you add what you want to it. It's good to know it.
Were there any favorite piano players down here? You had your mates like Earl Hines up there in Arkansas and all that time.

Oh yeah, well, his piano player that I liked around in New Orleans was Fats Pichon. I liked his playing until he was down there, worked with us down there by the Absinthe House. I was down there. I mean, after he went blind in there, I think that's about the best piano player I would've got. Well, my three was just him, and there was a piano player down here. He was pretty great too. Steve Lewis.
I was going to ask if you knew Steve Lewis. Yeah, he was a great piano player. I never got to know him.
He was a great piano player. Steve, Walter Pichon, all the guys that I met on the road, it was Oil Hines and Fats Waller.
Fats Waller, yeah.

Yeah. Now all the other guys came, I think, after those guys. They played styles, and they were similar to what they played. They had to build their own business for their business to build their business to build their and have a little freedom now to get around playing with different guys.

I think the first time I ever heard you, I remember George Lewis used to tell me, I began recording George back in 1943 even, and I'd be always asking him, I even stayed at his house a couple of summers, I'd come down for a month. So he told me about you, that you were one of the pianists, but I didn't get to hear you I believe until about 1950.

I worked with George, oh just like I told you, a whole year for this WTPS radio place, and we broadcast every Sunday, we had to go up there and rehearse this program every week for the Riga B account.
I remember that. Yeah. Subtle Stan was on that for a while too.
Yeah, and Walter Pichon was on there, well George stayed on there a year, and I stayed there with him.
And after that he started becoming, getting family,
well he started getting work, but he couldn't use me for the work, I mean because after all, I could make some of the jobs, then some of them I couldn't.
I couldn't work every day, and I couldn't work. Yeah, so I think he went back and got Alton Poinnell on, and went with him.

Yeah. I mean, now if I had, I'd been able to go along with him, I mean I would have been up there all along with him, and George Marrero, because I worked with the trumpet player name, we used to call him Cuckoo. Yeah, Talbert.
Talbert.
Talbert. In Howard, they were the two trumpet players, George Lewis, Lawrence Marrero, Jim Robinson.

I think I heard you the first time, it was across the river, along the west we go, along that road that goes up the river, with Ezreal Gorman one night, and Jim Robinson. I don't know, it wasn't anybody's special, organized band, it just happened to be a pickup band, but that's the first time I ever saw you and got to hear you. Then I didn't hear you for a few years, until you were here on Bourbon Street with George and all that. Yeah. I believe.
No, since I'm out freeing them, getting around, around there, and going there, I mean I have a chance. I think I'll make the trip with George, he want me to go to Japan.
Yeah, it'd be nice to make them those trips to England sometimes, just to see the rest of the world, as long as you're not tied down here.
And I have made some recordings too for, what you call it, over there in England, with Peter Bocard, I mean, I think Barry Martin.
Barry Martin. Yeah, he recorded me.

And he had sent for me last year, he wanted me to go to Japan in time with George and then left over there, but sometimes the deal fell through. He wanted me and Thomas and Emmanuel Paul was already in Europe, and I was supposed to meet them, but he called me the thing, fell through and it didn't come through.
Well, it'll be easier to start out from here. Yeah, yeah.

So I think I'll make, we'll go ahead and make the trip with George. I mean, because I might catch up on course. I mean, after you lost about 15 to 20 years lapsed in you, I mean, your thinking and your ideas and your development of your hands and your fingers, they're not the same.
But once you got that music and you don't forget it. You don't forget it. You don't forget it.
But you're not fast enough to execute them like when you were young. You have a lot of things in your mind to make, but you forget the age has gotten up with you, you see.
But then the experience is something that young people are going to do. Yeah, well, the experience is a whole lot of things.
I really had experience.
Well, I think if that's, unless there's something else you want to add? You know what? I think that's part of all.
Right up here to this future thing up here about making the trip to Japan. Well, that's, let's bring it out to Japan. So that's supposed to be about a month and a couple of weeks from now.
Well, I hope you get the next. Yeah.
